doc.title: Chuck Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 7, 2023

chapter: Growing up in Verona and Dry Jack
title: Making the Dry Jack LPs and the guitarist's departure
summary: Lamb shows the LPs Magical Elements and Whale City, recounts live studio recording with overdubs, and the guitarist leaving, which led him to Mike Demicco.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Would you mind holding up, I think those LPs are right there.
Oh yeah. So this was the first Dry Jack thing, “Magical Elements” and then “Whale City.”
And I was envious because everybody that had a band — unless you were strictly a part timer — was sort of trying to get to that level. Oh my God an LP, we got a record deal.
You got a record. Did it proceed from there as you hoped or what was it like dealing with a small record label?

Oh it was incredible. Maybe because of the small label thing but you know they just, there was no restrictions musically on what we were doing and there was a lot of freedom in the studio time-wise — just go ahead and make this record. But you know we had been playing — the only way we could make a record was to play live in the studio, which was trickier back then, the technology to do live and not have bleed with instruments and this kind of thing. But we basically played live in the studio and then I did my overdubs on my clavinet and my mini Moog and stuff. Right? Man, you know, it was great. And that band was — the guitar player, for personal reasons, left and moved back to Kansas City. So that ended — which was a drag because we were on a roll and we had just recorded a third album demo for Inner City which was called “Alien Intervention,” all this kind of wild stuff I had been composing. It was a really neat record. So then he left and then trying to create, you can’t re-create that vibe of what we had, no matter if you get the same instruments it doesn’t matter. So I just took that as a cue to start moving a little in a bit of a different direction. But I got Mike Demicco, who is the guitar player with me in the Brubeck Quartet and so I got him out of his gig at a hotel or something. So he was very grateful to be playing all of this great music. And then fast forward twenty years later he’s the one that said to Chris Brubeck, “Hey you’ve got to get Chuck Lamb.”
